subject: physics
prompt: A box is pushed along the floor. Tap the **normal force**, the force the floor exerts on the box.

image.alt: A box being pushed along a floor, with numbered markers on force arrows

hint: The surface pushes back on the box at right angles to itself.
explanation: The **normal force** is exerted by the surface on the object, acting **upwards, perpendicular to the surface**. On a level floor it balances the **gravitational force (weight)** acting downwards, so the box neither sinks into the floor nor rises off it. Its motion along the floor depends only on the horizontal net force.

subject: physics
prompt: Same box, same push. Tap the **force of friction** acting on the box.

image.alt: A box being pushed along a floor, with numbered markers on force arrows

hint: Friction acts where the two surfaces touch, against the direction of motion.
explanation: The **force of friction** acts along the surface where the bottom of the box touches the floor, in the direction **opposite to the motion**. The box speeds up only while the push is larger than friction. If you stop pushing, friction alone acts and brings the box to rest.

subject: physics
prompt: This is the velocity–time graph of a car on a straight road. Tap the part of the graph where the **net force on the car is zero**.

image.alt: Velocity-time graph of a car with numbered markers along the line

hint: Zero net force means zero acceleration. Where is the velocity not changing while the car moves?
explanation: Along **AB** the line is parallel to the time axis, so the velocity stays at $12\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and the acceleration is zero. By **Newton's first law**, a body moving with constant velocity has **no net force** on it (the engine's push just balances friction). Along OA and BC the velocity changes, so a net force acts. Point O is only an instant, not a stretch of motion.

subject: physics
prompt: Same car. Tap the part of the graph where the net force acts **opposite to the direction of motion**.

image.alt: Velocity-time graph of a car with numbered markers along the line

hint: A force against the motion makes the object slow down.
explanation: Along **BC** the velocity falls from $12\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ to zero, so the acceleration is **negative**. By **Newton's second law**, the acceleration is always in the direction of the net force, so here the net force points **backwards**, against the motion. Along OA the net force is forwards, and along AB it is zero.

subject: physics
prompt: Four objects move along straight lines. Tap the position–time graph of the object on which a **net force is acting**.

image.alt: Four position-time graphs for objects A, B, C and D, each with a numbered marker

hint: A straight position–time line means constant velocity. Look for the one whose slope keeps changing.
explanation: A net force produces **acceleration**, i.e. a changing velocity. On a position–time graph the slope is the velocity, so only the **curved graph of C**, which gets steeper and steeper, shows acceleration. A is at rest (flat line), and B and D are straight lines, so they move with **constant velocity**. Even D, moving backwards, has no net force on it.

subject: physics
prompt: The rocket's engine pushes hot gas downwards. Tap the arrow showing the force that the **exhaust gas exerts on the rocket**.

image.alt: A rocket lifting off, with numbered markers on arrows and parts

hint: By Newton's third law, this force is equal and opposite to the push of the rocket on the gas.
explanation: The engine pushes the gas **downwards** (the arrow in the exhaust). By **Newton's third law** the gas pushes the rocket **upwards** with an equal force. This pair acts on two different bodies, so it does not cancel. Because the upward push on the rocket is larger than its weight, the net force is upwards and the rocket lifts off.

subject: physics
prompt: Tap the force that actually **pushes the walker forward**.

image.alt: A person walking with numbered markers near the feet

hint: The force must act on the person, not on the ground.
explanation: While walking, your foot pushes the ground **backwards**. The ground pushes your foot **forwards** with an equal force, and this force is **friction**. So here friction helps motion instead of opposing it. The backward arrow acts on the ground, so it cannot move you; the normal force is upwards and balances your weight.

subject: physics
prompt: Two boxes joined by a string are pulled across a frictionless floor. Treat both boxes and the string as **one system**. Tap the only **external** horizontal force on the system.

image.alt: Two boxes joined by a string with numbered markers on the force arrows

hint: Forces that the parts of the system exert on each other are internal.
explanation: The **tension** forces are exerted by one part of the system on another (Box 1 and Box 2 via the string), so they are **internal** and form a third-law pair that cancels for the system. Only the **pull F** comes from outside. So the system accelerates as one body: $a = \dfrac{F}{m_1 + m_2}$.

subject: physics
prompt: The car in the graph has a mass of **1200 kg**. What is the net force on it from O to A (0 s to 4 s)?

image.alt: Velocity-time graph of a car rising from 0 to 12 m/s in 4 s, constant until 10 s, then falling to 0 at 16 s

hint: First find the acceleration from $v = u + at$, then use $F = ma$.
explanation: From the graph $u = 0$, $v = 12\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $t = 4\ \text{s}$, so $a = \dfrac{12 - 0}{4} = 3\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. $$F = ma = 1200 \times 3 = 3600\ \text{N}$$ in the direction of motion. 14,400 N multiplies the mass by the velocity instead of the acceleration, 400 N divides mass by acceleration, and 300 N divides mass by time.

subject: physics
prompt: The same **1200 kg** car is moving towards the east. What net force acts on it from B to C (10 s to 16 s)?

image.alt: Velocity-time graph of a car rising from 0 to 12 m/s in 4 s, constant until 10 s, then falling to 0 at 16 s

options.text: Zero, because the car is coming to rest

hint: The time interval is from 10 s to 16 s. A negative acceleration means the force points against the motion.
explanation: $u = 12\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $v = 0$, $t = 16 - 10 = 6\ \text{s}$, so $a = \dfrac{0 - 12}{6} = -2\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. $$F = ma = 1200 \times (-2) = -2400\ \text{N}$$ The minus sign means the force acts **opposite to the motion**, i.e. towards the west. 'East' is the sign slip, 1440 N uses $t = 10$ s read off the axis instead of the 6 s interval, and the car is slowing down, so the force is not zero.

subject: physics
prompt: A weightlifter holds a barbell steady above her head. The bar has a mass of **20 kg** and a **15 kg** plate is fixed on each side. What upward force must she apply? (Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.)

image.alt: A weightlifter holding a barbell with a plate on each side above her head

hint: Add up all the masses, find the weight with $F = mg$, and remember the forces must balance.
explanation: Total mass $= 20 + 15 + 15 = 50\ \text{kg}$. Weight $= mg = 50 \times 9.8 = 490\ \text{N}$ downwards. To keep the barbell steady the forces must be **balanced**, so she pushes **490 N upwards**. 343 N counts only one plate, 196 N counts only the bar, and 50 N is the mass, not a force.

subject: physics
prompt: A **20 kg** box rests on a floor. The largest friction the floor can provide is **40 N**. Meera pushes it with a steady **46 N**. How far does the box move in **3 s**?

image.alt: A box being pushed along a floor with force arrows

hint: Only the net force (push minus friction) accelerates the box. Then use $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$.
explanation: Net force $= 46 - 40 = 6\ \text{N}$, so $a = \dfrac{6}{20} = 0.3\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. $$s = 0 + \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.3 \times 3^2 = 1.35\ \text{m}$$ 2.7 m forgets the $\tfrac{1}{2}$, 0.45 m uses $t$ instead of $t^2$, and 10.35 m uses the full 46 N push and ignores friction. (A push of exactly 40 N would leave the box at rest.)

subject: physics
prompt: A gun of mass **4 kg** fires a bullet of mass **50 g** with a force of **6 N**. What is the initial acceleration of the **bullet**?

image.alt: Animation of a toy gun recoiling backwards as a bullet flies forwards, with arrows on each

hint: Convert grams to kilograms before using $a = \dfrac{F}{m}$.
explanation: $50\ \text{g} = 0.05\ \text{kg}$, so $a = \dfrac{6}{0.05} = 120\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. By **Newton's third law** the bullet pushes the gun back with the same 6 N, giving the gun only $\dfrac{6}{4} = 1.5\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ (that option is the gun's value). Equal forces, unequal masses, so unequal accelerations. 0.12 comes from using 50 kg, and 0.3 from multiplying force by mass.

subject: physics
prompt: In a snake boat (*Vallam kali*) practice, **120** oarsmen row. **112** of them row to push the boat forward, but **8** row the wrong way. Each applies **150 N**. What is the net force on the boat? (Ignore drag.)

image.alt: Animation of a long snake boat with many oarsmen rowing

hint: Forces in opposite directions subtract; the net force is along the larger one.
explanation: Forward force $= 112 \times 150 = 16{,}800\ \text{N}$; backward force $= 8 \times 150 = 1200\ \text{N}$. Net force $= 16{,}800 - 1200 = 15{,}600\ \text{N}$ forwards. 18,000 N adds all 120 oarsmen, 16,800 N ignores the wrong-way rowers, and 14,400 N subtracts them twice.

subject: physics
prompt: A **20 g** bullet moving at $200\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ enters a heavy wooden block and stops after going **10 cm** into it. Assuming constant deceleration, estimate the stopping force on the bullet.

image.alt: Animation of a bullet entering a wooden block and stopping inside it

hint: Use $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with $v = 0$, in SI units, then $F = ma$.
explanation: $m = 0.02\ \text{kg}$, $s = 0.1\ \text{m}$. $$0 = 200^2 + 2a(0.1) \Rightarrow a = -\dfrac{40\,000}{0.2} = -2{,}00{,}000\ \text{m s}^{-2}$$ $F = 0.02 \times 2{,}00{,}000 = 4000\ \text{N}$, opposing the motion. 40 N keeps 10 cm unconverted, 40,00,000 N uses 20 g as 20 kg, and 8000 N drops the 2 in $2as$.

subject: physics
prompt: A footballer kicks a **0.45 kg** ball from rest to **72 km/h** with an average force of **600 N**. For how long was the boot in contact with the ball?

image.alt: Animation of a boot kicking a football across the grass

hint: Convert km/h to m/s (× 5/18). Find $a = F/m$, then $t = (v - u)/a$.
explanation: $72 \times \dfrac{5}{18} = 20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. $a = \dfrac{600}{0.45} \approx 1333\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, so $$t = \dfrac{20 - 0}{1333} = 0.015\ \text{s}$$ (equivalently $t = \dfrac{mv}{F} = \dfrac{0.45 \times 20}{600}$). 0.054 s uses 72 without converting, 66.7 s turns the fraction upside down, and 13.5 s multiplies force by mass.

subject: physics
prompt: A **4 kg** block slides at a steady $6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ onto a rough patch where friction is **5 N**. At the same moment an extra **3 N** force opposing the motion is applied. How far does it go before stopping?

image.alt: Animation of a block sliding from a smooth floor onto a rough patch and stopping, with two backward arrows

hint: Both forces act against the motion, so add them. Then use $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$.
explanation: Net opposing force $= 5 + 3 = 8\ \text{N}$, so $a = -\dfrac{8}{4} = -2\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. $$0 = 6^2 - 2 \times 2 \times s \Rightarrow s = \dfrac{36}{4} = 9\ \text{m}$$ 14.4 m uses friction alone, 36 m subtracts the two forces (2 N), and 18 m forgets the 2 in $2as$.

subject: physics
prompt: A tractor's net pull F gives a harrow an acceleration of $3\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, and gives a trolley $6\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. With the harrow loaded on the trolley, what acceleration does the same force F produce? (Ignore friction.)

image.alt: Animation of a tractor pulling a trolley that carries a harrow

hint: Write each mass as $m = F/a$, add the masses, then divide F by the total.
explanation: $m_1 = \dfrac{F}{3}$ and $m_2 = \dfrac{F}{6}$, so $$a = \dfrac{F}{m_1 + m_2} = \dfrac{a_1 a_2}{a_1 + a_2} = \dfrac{3 \times 6}{3 + 6} = 2\ \text{m s}^{-2}$$ A bigger mass must give a **smaller** acceleration than either alone, which rules out adding (9), averaging (4.5) or subtracting (3) the accelerations.

subject: physics
prompt: In the picture, Box 1 has mass **4 kg** and Box 2 has mass **2 kg**. A force of **30 N** pulls Box 1 on a frictionless floor. What is the acceleration of the boxes?

image.alt: Two boxes joined by a string on a smooth floor, pulled to the right

hint: Treat the two boxes and the string as one system; the string's tension is internal.
explanation: The whole system moves together, so $$a = \dfrac{F}{m_1 + m_2} = \dfrac{30}{4 + 2} = 5\ \text{m s}^{-2}$$ 7.5 uses only Box 1's mass, 15 uses only Box 2's, and 180 multiplies instead of dividing.

subject: physics
prompt: Two friends push a stalled **900 kg** car in the same direction with **300 N** and **240 N**. Friction on the car is **360 N**. What is the car's acceleration?

image.alt: Two people pushing a stalled car from behind

hint: Forces in the same direction add; friction acts against them.
explanation: Pushes in the same direction add: $300 + 240 = 540\ \text{N}$. Net force $= 540 - 360 = 180\ \text{N}$, so $a = \dfrac{180}{900} = 0.2\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. 0.6 ignores friction, 0.067 subtracts the two pushes, and 1.0 adds friction as if it helped.

subject: physics
prompt: In the cart-and-cup activity, the cart takes $T_1 = 3.0$ s to cross the table. With double the mass in the cup it takes $T_2 = 2.2$ s over the same distance, starting from rest. What is $\dfrac{a_2}{a_1}$?

image.alt: Animation of a cart on a table pulled by a thread over a pipe to a falling paper cup

hint: From $s = \frac{1}{2}aT^2$ with the same $s$, $a_1T_1^2 = a_2T_2^2$.
explanation: $$\dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac{T_1^2}{T_2^2} = \dfrac{9.0}{4.84} \approx 1.86$$ Doubling the force nearly doubles the acceleration; it falls a little short of 2 because of **friction** at the wheels and measurement errors. 1.36 forgets to square the times, while 0.54 and 0.73 turn the ratio upside down.

subject: physics
prompt: **Momentum** is mass × velocity. What is the momentum of a **160 g** cricket ball moving at **90 km/h**?

image.alt: Animation of a fielder's hands catching a cricket ball

hint: Use SI units: kg and m/s. 1 km/h = 5/18 m/s.
explanation: $m = 0.16\ \text{kg}$ and $v = 90 \times \dfrac{5}{18} = 25\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, so $p = mv = 0.16 \times 25 = 4\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$, in the direction of the velocity. 14.4 keeps km/h, 4000 keeps grams, and 0.0064 divides mass by velocity. The more complete form of Newton's second law says the **rate of change of momentum** is proportional to the net force.

subject: physics
prompt: The bus brakes suddenly and the standing passenger tips **forwards**. Why?

image.alt: Animation of a bus braking while a standing passenger tips forwards

options.text: The brakes push the passenger forwards
Her upper body tends to keep moving with its earlier velocity while her feet slow down with the bus
The air inside the bus pushes her forwards

hint: Objects resist changes to their state of motion.
explanation: Newton called the tendency of objects to resist a change in their state of rest or uniform motion **inertia**. Friction from the floor slows her feet along with the bus, but no such force acts directly on her upper body, so it carries on forwards as **Newton's first law** says. No new forward force appears.

subject: physics
prompt: A sailor jumps forwards from a small boat onto the shore. What happens to the boat?

image.alt: Animation of a sailor jumping from a small boat towards the shore

options.text: It moves forwards towards the shore with the sailor
It moves backwards, away from the shore
It only bobs up and down

hint: To jump forwards, the sailor's feet must push on something.
explanation: To jump forwards, the sailor's feet push the boat **backwards**. By **Newton's third law** the boat pushes the sailor forwards with an equal force. These forces act on different bodies, so the boat, floating freely on water, moves **backwards, away from the shore**.

subject: physics
prompt: Two identical spring balances are hooked together. One end is fixed to a wall and you pull the other. The left balance reads **8 N**. What does the right balance read?

image.alt: Two spring balances hooked together between a wall and a hand; the right scale is hidden

hint: Each balance measures the force the other balance applies on it.
explanation: The two balances pull on each other with forces that are **equal in magnitude and opposite in direction**, so both read **8 N** however hard you pull. This activity checks **Newton's third law**. 16 N wrongly adds the readings and 4 N wrongly shares the force between them.

prompt: An object is **already moving** and **no net force** acts on it. Which velocity–time graph describes its motion?

Velocity-time graph: a straight line sloping down
Velocity-time graph: a horizontal line above the time axis

hint: No net force means no acceleration.
explanation: By **Newton's first law**, an object in motion keeps moving with **constant velocity** unless a net force acts. So its velocity–time graph is a **horizontal line above the time axis** (Graph R), and its position–time graph would be a straight sloping line. P shows speeding up and Q slowing down, which both need a net force.

Force-mass graph: a straight line rising from the origin

subject: physics
prompt: A hand cart loaded with vegetables collides with an identical empty cart. During the collision:

image.alt: Animation of a loaded hand cart and an empty hand cart rolling into each other

options.text: the loaded cart pushes harder on the empty cart
the empty cart pushes harder on the loaded cart
neither cart exerts a force on the other
each cart exerts a force of equal magnitude on the other

hint: Forces always come in pairs.
explanation: By **Newton's third law**, the forces the two carts exert on each other are **equal in magnitude and opposite in direction**, whatever their masses. The *effects* differ: the lighter empty cart gets the larger acceleration, which is why it seems to be hit 'harder'.

subject: physics
prompt: Like the Vikram lander of **Chandrayaan-3**, this lander is moving down towards the Moon and must slow down for a soft landing. Which way should its engine push out the exhaust gas?

image.alt: Animation of a lander descending towards the Moon's surface, with an arrow showing its downward motion

options.text: Downwards, in the direction it is moving
Sideways, at right angles to its motion
It need not fire; with no air it slows down by itself

hint: The gas pushes back on the lander in the opposite direction to the way the gas is thrown.
explanation: If the engine fires gas **in the direction of motion** (downwards), the gas pushes the lander **upwards**, against its motion, by **Newton's third law**. This slows it down, which is how Vikram landed softly near the Moon's south pole. Firing upwards would speed it up, and nothing slows it 'by itself'.

subject: physics
prompt: A wooden block is pulled along a table at a **constant velocity**. The spring balance reads **3 N**. What is the force of friction on the block?

image.alt: Animation of a wooden block pulled along a table by a spring balance

options.text: 0 N, because the block is not accelerating

hint: Constant velocity means the net force is zero.
explanation: At **constant velocity** the net force is zero, so the pull and friction are **balanced**: friction is **3 N** acting opposite to the pull. That is why a spring balance can measure friction. The block not accelerating means the net force is zero, not that friction is zero.

subject: physics
prompt: On a smooth floor, block P has forces of **5 N** and **4 N** acting in opposite directions, while block Q slides at **constant velocity**. Which statement is correct?

image.alt: Block P with a 5 N arrow to the left and a 4 N arrow to the right; block Q sliding to the right

options.text: P has a net force on it; Q does not
Q has a net force on it; P does not
Both P and Q have a net force on them
Neither P nor Q has a net force on it

hint: Unequal opposite forces leave something over. Constant velocity means nothing is left over.
explanation: On P the forces are **unbalanced**: net force $= 5 - 4 = 1\ \text{N}$ towards the 5 N side, so P accelerates. Q moves with **constant velocity**, so by Newton's first law the net force on it is **zero**. A moving object does not need a net force to keep moving.

prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

assertion: A girl sitting on a wheeled chair rolls backwards when she pushes a heavy table forwards.
reason: The table exerts a force on the girl that is equal and opposite to her push on the table.
hint: Who pushes the girl?
explanation: Both are true and R explains A. By **Newton's third law** the table pushes back on her with an equal and opposite force, and this force acts on **her**, so she and the chair roll backwards. If she pulled the table instead, she would roll towards it.

image.alt: A fruit falling from a tree towards the Earth, with an arrow on the fruit and an arrow on the Earth

assertion: A falling fruit moves towards the Earth, but the Earth's motion towards the fruit is far too small to notice.
reason: The fruit pulls the Earth with a much smaller force than the Earth pulls the fruit.
hint: Compare the forces first, then compare the masses.
explanation: A is true, R is false. By **Newton's third law** the Earth and the fruit pull each other with forces of **equal** magnitude. The Earth's mass is enormous, so by $a = \dfrac{F}{m}$ its acceleration is extremely small, while the fruit's is large.

prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Animation of a passenger moving forwards into an inflating airbag

assertion: Airbags lower the risk of serious injury when a vehicle stops abruptly in a collision.
reason: The soft cushion increases the time over which the passenger is brought to rest, so the acceleration and hence the force on the passenger are smaller.
hint: Think about how $F = ma$ changes when the same change in velocity happens more slowly.
explanation: Both are true and R explains A. The passenger's velocity must drop to zero either way. Spreading that change over a **longer time** means a **smaller acceleration**, and by $F = ma$ a **smaller force**. Seat belts add to this protection. A fielder pulling the hands back while catching uses the same idea.

image.alt: Animation of a bar magnet near a compass whose needle swings

assertion: A bar magnet exerts a larger magnetic force on a compass needle than the needle exerts on the magnet.
reason: For the same force, an object with a smaller mass gets a larger acceleration.
hint: Is the third law only for contact forces?

The needle swings while the magnet stays put because the light needle gets a large acceleration from that force, while the much heavier magnet (held in a hand) does not.

prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A canoeist paddling, with two arrows at the paddle blade

assertion: A canoe speeds up more when the canoeist pushes the water backwards harder.
reason: The paddle's push on the water and the water's push on the paddle act on different objects.
hint: R is true, but does it say anything about *pushing harder*?
explanation: Both are true, but R does not explain A. R explains why the action–reaction pair does **not cancel**. A is explained by the size of the force: a harder push on the water means a **larger forward push** of the water on the paddle and canoe, so by the second law a larger acceleration.

subject: physics
prompt: **No net force** acts on an object. Which of these are possible? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Animation of a ball rolling down a ramp and along a long, smooth horizontal surface

options.text: It stays at rest, if it was at rest
It keeps moving with constant velocity, if it was moving
It moves with a constant acceleration
It moves round a circle at a steady speed

hint: Zero net force means zero acceleration, and velocity includes direction.
explanation: By **Newton's first law**, with zero net force an object at rest **stays at rest** and a moving object **keeps the same velocity**. Speeding up or any constant acceleration needs a net force. Going round a circle changes the **direction** of velocity, so it needs a net force too. In the 17th century **Galileo** argued through thought experiments that a ball on a perfectly smooth horizontal plane would keep moving forever.

subject: physics
prompt: Which of these **reduce the force** on a moving object by making it stop over a **longer time**? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Animation of a high jumper going over a bar and sinking into a thick mat

options.text: An airbag inflating in front of a passenger
Cracking a coconut by striking it hard on a stone
A thick landing mat or sand bed for high jumpers
A fielder drawing the hands back while catching
Packing glassware in bubble wrap or hay

hint: Look for soft, give-way surfaces or movements.
explanation: The airbag, landing mat, drawn-back hands and bubble wrap all **increase the stopping time**, so the deceleration is smaller and, by $F = ma$, the force is smaller. Cracking a coconut does the **opposite**: it stops in a very short time, so the ground exerts a huge force that breaks the shell. Tyre treads increase friction, which is a different idea.

subject: physics
prompt: Which of these **increase** friction? Select all that apply.

image.alt: A shoe sole with grooves and a turning tyre with treads

options.text: Grooves on the soles of footwear
Oiling the moving parts of a machine
Giving a vehicle a streamlined shape
Wrapping a rope one more turn round a post to hold a load
Magnetic levitation of a train above its track

hint: Three of these help us grip; three help things slip.
explanation: **Grooves** on soles and **treads** on tyres increase friction so we can walk and drive safely, which is why wet polished floors, ice and waterlogged roads are risky. Each extra **turn of rope** round a post increases the grip a lot, which is how ships are held at a pier. Lubricants, streamlining and magnetic levitation are ways scientists **reduce** friction.

subject: physics
prompt: Which of these statements are **true**? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Animation of a handlebar turning, with an arrow at each end

options.text: Equal and opposite forces at the two ends of a handlebar can make it turn
Newton's laws need changes for speeds close to the speed of light
Newton's laws work for everyday objects but not for planets and stars
The air's friction on a box pushed across a room is always too large to ignore
To find the acceleration of two boxes tied together, the tension in the string need not be considered

hint: Two of the false statements underestimate or overestimate Newton's laws and air.
explanation: (a) True: equal and opposite forces on the two ends of an **extended object** like a handlebar or tap make it **rotate**. (b) True: Newton's laws need modification very close to massive objects, near the speed of light and at atomic scales. (c) False: they describe motion from everyday objects to planets and stars. (d) False: air friction is often so small it can be neglected. (e) True: tension is an **internal force** of the system.

explanation: Block 1: both forces point right, so $10 + 6 = 16\ \text{N}$ right. Block 2: $10 - 6 = 4\ \text{N}$ along the 10 N force, to the right. Block 3: the 10 N force points left, so $4\ \text{N}$ left. Block 4: 8 N each way, so the forces are **balanced** and the net force is zero.

subject: physics
prompt: A ball rolls on a smooth, **frictionless** surface. Match each condition with what happens to the ball.

image.alt: Animation of a ball rolling along a long, smooth horizontal surface

left.text: No net force acts on it
A net force acts in its direction of motion
A net force acts opposite to its direction of motion

hint: The acceleration always points the same way as the net force.
explanation: With **no net force**, the velocity stays the same (first law), even with no push. A net force **along** the motion gives an acceleration along the motion, so the speed **increases**. A net force **against** the motion **decreases** the speed gradually; nothing stops instantly.

subject: physics
prompt: Match each **action** with its **reaction** force.

image.alt: Animation of a person climbing a coconut tree

left.text: A rocket engine pushes gas downwards
A climber's legs push down on the tree trunk
A fire hose pushes a jet of water forwards

right.text: Friction from the trunk pushes the climber up
The water pushes the hose backwards
The water pushes the paddle forwards
The gas pushes the rocket upwards

hint: The reaction is equal and opposite, and acts on the first object.
explanation: Each reaction is **equal and opposite** to its action and acts on the object that did the pushing. That is why the canoe moves forwards, the rocket rises, the climber goes up (harder on smooth trunks with less friction), and a fireperson has to struggle to hold a hose that is pushed **backwards**.

prompt: How big is a newton? Arrange these forces from **smallest to largest**.

image.alt: An open palm holding a small 100 g mass

items.text: Net force on a 1500 kg car accelerating at $2\ \text{m s}^{-2}$
A light touch (about $10^{-3}$ N)
Holding a 30 kg barbell steady
The tiniest force measured in special experiments (about $10^{-24}$ N)
Your palm holding up a 100 g mass

hint: Work out the last three with $F = mg$ or $F = ma$.
explanation: Yoctonewtons ($10^{-24}$ N) < a light touch, about a **millinewton** ($10^{-3}$ N) < a 100 g mass, about $0.1 \times 9.8 \approx 1$ N < a 30 kg barbell, $30 \times 9.8 = 294$ N < the car, $1500 \times 2 = 3000$ N.

prompt: Arrange the steps of the cart-and-cup activity, which tests how force affects acceleration.

image.alt: Animation of a cart on a table pulled by a thread over a pipe to a paper cup

items.text: Read the time $T_1$ from the slow-motion video
Fit pencil axles and wheels to a cardboard box to make a cart
Double the mass in the cup and repeat to find $T_2$
Pass the thread over the pipe and hang the paper cup
Release the cart from the start line while recording a slow-motion video
Measure the mass of the cup with the objects in it

hint: Build and set up, measure, run, read, then change one thing.
explanation: Build the cart, set up the thread, pipe and cup, **measure** the cup's mass, run the cart while filming, read $T_1$, then **double the force** (the cup's mass) and repeat for $T_2$. Since $a_2/a_1 = T_1^2/T_2^2$, you find a larger force gives a larger acceleration for the same mass.

prompt: Arrange the steps to make the **balloon rocket** in the correct order.

image.alt: Animation of a balloon taped to a straw moving along a taut thread

items.text: Pass a long thread through the straw and tie its ends to two nails, keeping it taut
Untie the balloon's neck and watch which way it moves
Inflate the balloon and tie its neck with a small piece of thread
Tape a piece of straw to the balloon, pointing towards its neck

hint: You need a balloon full of air before you can attach it to anything.
explanation: Inflate and tie the balloon, tape on the straw, thread it on a taut line and then let the air out. The stretched balloon pushes the air out backwards and the air pushes the balloon **forwards** with an equal force (**third law**), the same way a rocket works.

prompt: You want the stopping force on a bullet that stops inside a wooden block. Arrange the steps of the working in order.

image.alt: Animation of a bullet entering a wooden block and stopping inside it

items.text: Multiply by the mass to get the force, $F = ma$
Convert the mass to kg and the distance to m
State that the force acts opposite to the bullet's motion
Use $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with $v = 0$ to find the deceleration

hint: You cannot use $F = ma$ until you know $a$.
explanation: Work in **SI units** first (g → kg, cm → m). Then the kinematic equation $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ gives the deceleration, $F = ma$ turns it into a force, and the negative sign of $a$ tells you the force **opposes the motion**.
